explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Hezekiah, Judah's king, doesn't go solo on this one. The text says he consulted with his leaders and mighty men, and they helped him carry the plan out (2 Chronicles 32:3). Even a king can use a good team.

That's right, friend. When Hezekiah, Judah's king, sees Sennacherib has come to make war against Jerusalem, he consults with his leaders and mighty men. Then they help him carry the plan out (2 Chronicles 32:3). Wise folks ask for help, and I've learned that the hard way, usually after the dough is already on the floor.

Yes, friend. The plan is to stop up the waters of the springs outside the city (2 Chronicles 32:3). Hezekiah consulted with his leaders and mighty men about it, and they helped him carry it out. Then many people assembled and stopped up all the springs and the stream that flowed through the land (2 Chronicles 32:4).

Guards would be a fine idea in some other story, friend. But the text says the plan was about stopping up the waters of the springs (2 Chronicles 32:3). Nobody is told to stand next to a spring and look serious. They shut the water off.

That's the opposite direction, friend. The text says the plan was about stopping up the waters of the springs outside the city (2 Chronicles 32:3). Hezekiah was closing things off, not digging them out.

explanations.answer: So Assyria won't find plenty of water
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The people say it themselves: “Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?” (2 Chronicles 32:4). That's why they stopped up all the springs and the stream. I think that's a plan with a pretty big thirst behind it.

explanations.answer: So Jerusalem's wells will stay full
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but the text never mentions wells. The people give their own reason: “Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?” (2 Chronicles 32:4). The goal was what the Assyrians would find outside, not what Jerusalem would keep inside.

explanations.answer: So the enemy can't cross the stream
explanations.explanation: I can see how you got there, friend, but crossing isn't in this verse. The people say, “Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?” (2 Chronicles 32:4). The worry was the water the Assyrian kings would find, not whether they could wade over it.
Right on, friend. Hezekiah rebuilds the broken sections of the wall and raises towers on it. Then he also builds an outer wall (2 Chronicles 32:5). He didn't stop at the repairs.

Not this time, friend. The text says Hezekiah rebuilt the broken sections of the wall and raised up towers. He ALSO built an outer wall (2 Chronicles 32:5). That's an outer wall in addition to the repairs.
That's the one, baker. Hezekiah produced an abundance of weapons and shields (2 Chronicles 32:5). Walls, towers, terraces and now gear for the people to hold. The man did not do half a job.
That sounds like an army, friend, but the text doesn't list any. What Hezekiah produced in abundance was weapons and shields (2 Chronicles 32:5). Chariots and horses never come up in this verse.
That's a nice pile, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says Hezekiah produced an abundance of weapons and shields (2 Chronicles 32:5). Gold and silver aren't on that list.

Yes, baker. Hezekiah says, “…there is a greater One with us than with him.” (2 Chronicles 32:7). Then he says who: the LORD their God (2 Chronicles 32:8). Their courage rests on who is with them, not on how big the crowd is.

explanations.answer: Their army is bigger than his
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Hezekiah does talk about the vast army with the king of Assyria (2 Chronicles 32:7), but he never compares the two armies. His reason is, “…there is a greater One with us than with him.” Then he says who: the LORD our God (2 Chronicles 32:8).

explanations.answer: Their walls are too strong for him
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah did build up the walls, friend, but that's not what he tells the people. He says, “…there is a greater One with us than with him.” (2 Chronicles 32:7). Bricks are good, but he points to the One who is with them.

The text says the opposite, friend. After the speech, “…the people were strengthened by the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.” (2 Chronicles 32:8). They walked away stronger, not shaken. That's a pep talk that actually worked, unlike the ones I give my mixing bowls.

That's right, friend. The text says, “…the people were strengthened by the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.” (2 Chronicles 32:8). He pointed them to the LORD, and they came away stronger. Good words can do that.

That's it, baker. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, asks, “What is the basis of your confidence, that you remain in Jerusalem under siege?” (2 Chronicles 32:10). He starts by trying to poke at what they're trusting. I think that's the first crack he's hoping to make.

Anger is a fair guess, friend, but the question is about something else. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, asks, “What is the basis of your confidence, that you remain in Jerusalem under siege?” (2 Chronicles 32:10). He wants them doubting what they trust.

Sorrow would be a softer message, friend, and this one isn't soft. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, asks, “What is the basis of your confidence, that you remain in Jerusalem under siege?” (2 Chronicles 32:10). The question aims straight at what the people are leaning on.

Yes, baker. Sennacherib quotes Hezekiah saying, “You must worship before one altar, and on it you shall burn sacrifices…” (2 Chronicles 32:12). Remember, this is Sennacherib's telling of it. He's presenting it as something to hold against Hezekiah.

Gates are a creative guess, friend. But Sennacherib's own words are, “You must worship before one altar, and on it you shall burn sacrifices…” (2 Chronicles 32:12). One altar, not a bunch of spots around the city.

That's the opposite of what Sennacherib reports, friend. He says Hezekiah told them, “You must worship before one altar, and on it you shall burn sacrifices…” (2 Chronicles 32:12). One altar, not one in every town.

explanations.answer: Not one could deliver its people
explanations.explanation: That's the boast, baker. Sennacherib asks, “Who among all the gods of these nations that my fathers devoted to destruction has been able to deliver his people from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14). He's claiming not one of those gods has done it. Then he asks, “How then can your God deliver you from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14).

explanations.answer: Some held him off for a while
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Sennacherib asks who among those gods “…has been able to deliver his people from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14). His claim is that not one of them has delivered his people. Holding him off for a while isn't part of what he says.

explanations.answer: A few won battles against him
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Sennacherib asks, “Who among all the gods of these nations…has been able to deliver his people from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14). His claim is that none of those gods has been able to deliver his people. Battles won against him aren't what he's talking about.

That's right, friend. The text says Sennacherib “…wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel…” (2 Chronicles 17). His servants had also spoken further against the LORD God (2 Chronicles 32:16), and he put his own mocking in writing.

Not quite, friend. The text says Sennacherib “…wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel…” (2 Chronicles 32:17). His servants also spoke further against the LORD God (2 Chronicles 32:16), but the letters are his.

explanations.answer: To terrify them and capture the city
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. The Assyrians called out loudly in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall “…to frighten and terrify them in order to capture the city.” (2 Chronicles 32:18). I think that would be a hard thing to hear from up there.

explanations.answer: To offer them a peace deal
explanations.explanation: A peace deal would be nice, friend, but that's not what this shouting is. The text says it was “…to frighten and terrify them in order to capture the city.” (2 Chronicles 32:18). No offer comes with it, just fear.

explanations.answer: To call Hezekiah out to fight
explanations.explanation: The shouting is aimed at someone else, friend. The Assyrians call out to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall (2 Chronicles 32:18). The reason is “…to frighten and terrify them in order to capture the city.” No duel is mentioned.

That's the phrase, baker. The text says the Assyrians spoke against the God of Jerusalem as they had spoken against the gods of the peoples of the earth, “…the work of human hands.” (2 Chronicles 32:19). Those gods were made by people. God is the One who created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1).
Good try, friend, but those words aren't in this verse. The text calls the gods of the peoples of the earth “…the work of human hands.” (2 Chronicles 32:19). They were things people made.
I get the sky idea, friend, because I love a good night sky. But this verse calls those gods “…the work of human hands.” (2 Chronicles 32:19). They came from human hands, not from the heavens.

Not what the text says, friend. In response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, “…cried out to heaven in prayer…” (2 Chronicles 32:20). Nobody marches out here. They take it to the LORD.

That's right, friend. The text says Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, “…cried out to heaven in prayer…” (2 Chronicles 32:20). No army leaves the city in this verse. They answer all that shouting by calling out to God.

Yes, baker. King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah cried out to heaven in prayer (2 Chronicles 32:20). Then the LORD “…sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria.” (2 Chronicles 32:21). The prayer goes up, and the answer comes down.

Hail shows up in other Bible stories, friend, like in Exodus 9:23, but not this one. Here the text says the LORD sent an angel into the Assyrian camp (2 Chronicles 32:21). The answer to the prayer was an angel.

Hornets are scary, friend, but they're not in this passage. The text says Hezekiah and Isaiah cried out to heaven in prayer (2 Chronicles 32:20). Then the LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp (2 Chronicles 32:21).

Opposite, friend. The text says that from then on Hezekiah “…was exalted in the eyes of all nations.” (2 Chronicles 32:23). Many brought offerings to Jerusalem for the LORD and valuable gifts for Hezekiah. The nations lifted him up instead of looking down.

That's right, friend. The text says Hezekiah “…was exalted in the eyes of all nations.” (2 Chronicles 32:23). Gifts came to him and offerings came to Jerusalem for the LORD. That's the opposite of looking down on him.
